title: Dystopias
objective: After this level you can compare how Brave New World and Nineteen Eighty-Four imagine a society controlled by pleasure or by fear.
summary: Dystopias flip More's utopia into warnings. Huxley's Brave New World (1932) controls people by pleasure; Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), by fear.

cards.headline: Two nightmares of the future: one keeps you scared, one keeps you happy.
cards.body: Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932) and George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) both imagine a society under total control. They disagree about how it's done. That disagreement is the key to reading them.

cards.headline: The opposite of utopia
cards.body: Thomas More coined the word utopia in his 1516 book of that name, a play on Greek meaning both "good place" and "no place". A dystopian novel flips it: a fictional society of dehumanization, fear and oppression. Dystopias often work as cautionary tales, taking trends of their own day and projecting them into a grim future. Britannica calls these two novels great didactic landmarks.

cards.headline: Huxley: control by pleasure
cards.body: In Brave New World, citizens are sorted as embryos into castes, from Alphas to Epsilons, and conditioned to fit their roles. Nobody has to be dragged anywhere. A pleasure-giving drug, soma, keeps everyone content and compliant. The prison is comfortable, and that's the horror.

cards.headline: Orwell: control by fear
cards.body: Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four as a warning against totalitarianism. The Party rules through the Thought Police and continual surveillance, and posters remind everyone that Big Brother is watching. Its invented language, Newspeak, is designed to limit free thought. Here obedience comes from fear.

cards.fact: One fears what we hate. One fears what we love.
cards.context: In Amusing Ourselves to Death (1985), the critic Neil Postman set the two side by side. Orwell feared people who would ban books; Huxley feared that no one would want to read them anyway. Orwell's danger is something we hate. Huxley's is something we love.

mascot.line: Keep this pair: Orwell, control by fear. Huxley, control by pleasure.

cards.headline: Dystopias: decoded
learned: Utopia: More's good place that is no place
Huxley: control by pleasure and soma
Orwell: control by fear and surveillance

questions.prompt: In Brave New World, what keeps citizens content?

options.label: Newspeak, a language that limits thought

questions.explanation: Huxley's World State keeps its conditioned citizens content and compliant with the drug soma.

questions.prompt: Imagine a society where nobody bans books, but endless entertainment means nobody reads them. By Postman's reading, whose fear is that?

options.label: Orwell's: control by what we hate
options.rationale: Orwell feared those who would ban books.

options.label: Huxley's: control by what we love
More's: a perfect good place
options.rationale: Utopia is the dream, not the nightmare.

questions.explanation: Postman: Huxley feared no one would want to read, ruined by what we love; Orwell feared those who would ban books.

questions.prompt: Level 2's fables poke at human follies and carry a lesson. What do dystopian novels do that is similar?

options.label: Use talking animals to state a moral
Describe a perfect society to copy
Warn readers by projecting today's trends into a grim future

questions.explanation: Like fables, dystopias teach: they are cautionary tales, projecting current trends into a grim future.
